summary: Gives guidance for locating the resources associated with the im and pres URI schemes defined by the Common Profiles for Presence and Instant Messaging. It explains how to resolve these addresses to find the right service.

plainLanguage.summary: An instant messaging address such as im:fred@example.com names a person but not the server to contact. This RFC explains how the client finds that server. It looks up a DNS SRV record whose name is built from the service, the protocol and the domain, and falls back to the domain's address record when no such record exists.

questions: how to find an instant messaging server from an im uri
how to resolve an im uri
what is the pres uri scheme
how does srv lookup work for instant messaging
subtitle: How a client turns an im: or pres: address into the server to contact, using DNS SRV records.

tldr.problem: The im and pres URI schemes name an instant inbox or a presence, but a client still has to find the server that handles the domain in that address.
tldr.mechanism: The client looks up DNS SRV records whose Service label is _im or _pres and whose Protocol label names the messaging protocol, for example _im._bip.example.com., and falls back to the domain's A record, treated as an implicit SRV record with preference 0, when no SRV record exists.
tldr.outcome: A successful lookup can return several servers, and the client must be able to try them in order and should try at least two. IANA keeps two registries of Protocol labels, one for instant messaging and one for presence.

today: RFC 3861 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2004, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the description of how im and pres URIs are located through DNS SRV records.

sections.title: Two URI Schemes That Need Looking Up
sections.content:
Presence and instant messaging are defined in RFC 2778. The Common Profiles for Presence (CPP) and Instant Messaging (CPIM) define two URI schemes: im for INSTANT INBOXes and pres for PRESENTITIES. This document provides rules for locating the resources associated with URIs that use these schemes through the Domain Name Service, and it notes that the same rules could be applied to other URI schemes.

Both profiles define operations with source and destination attributes. Many instant messaging and presence protocols let those attributes hold URIs, and the im and pres schemes let such protocols express the identity of the principals taking part in an exchange. When an operation passes through a CPIM or CPP gateway, these URIs can be relayed without modification, which helps interoperability.
sections.plainLanguage: Two kinds of address are defined here. An im address points at an instant inbox, where messages arrive for a person. A pres address points at a presence, where a person's current status is published. The address says who, but not where the server is.

sections.title: Building the Name to Look Up
sections.content:
A client determines the address of a suitable server on behalf of the system named by the domain, by resolving the destination domain name to either an intermediate relay system or a final target system. Only resolvable, fully-qualified domain names are permitted in an IM URI.

The symbolic name used in the Service field of the SRV record is _im for instant messaging and _pres for presence, matching the URI schemes. The advertisement is incomplete if it does not name the protocol that will carry the operations, so the Protocol field of the SRV record holds an IANA-registered label for the underlying instant messaging or presence protocol.

Taking the IM URI as a concrete example, a lookup is performed for SRV records for the target domain, the desired service using the _im Service label and the desired IM transfer protocol. If the destination INSTANT INBOX is im:fred@example.com and the sender wishes to use an IM transfer protocol called BIP, with _bip registered with IANA as a valid Protocol label for the IM Service, then the SRV lookup is performed for _im._bip.example.com. The same procedure is used for PRES URIs with the _pres Service label.

Some clients support several instant messaging or presence protocols. In that case they may make several such SRV queries, in an application-specific order, until they find one that is supported in common with the target domain.
sections.plainLanguage: The client builds one DNS name out of three parts and looks it up. The first part says what is wanted, _im for messaging or _pres for presence. The second part names the chat protocol, so a client that speaks a different protocol can ask for its own. The third part is the domain from the address. The example in the RFC looks up _im._bip.example.com. for the address im:fred@example.com.

sections.title: Looking Up the Domain
sections.content:
Once a client identifies the domain to which operations will be delivered, a DNS lookup MUST be performed to resolve the domain. The names MUST be fully-qualified domain names, and the mechanisms for inferring a fully-qualified name from a partial name or a local alias are a local matter.

The lookup first attempts to locate SRV resource records associated with the domain. If a canonical name (CNAME) record is found instead, the resulting domain is processed as if it were the initial domain. If one or more SRV records are found, a sender MUST NOT use any A records associated with that domain unless they are located through the SRV records. If no SRV records are found but an A record is found, then the A record is treated as if it was associated with an implicit SRV record, with a preference of 0, pointing to that domain.
sections.plainLanguage: The client asks the DNS for the service records first. If the answer redirects to another name, that name is looked up instead. When service records exist, the plain address record of the domain is ignored unless the service records point at it. When no service record exists, the address record is used on its own, with priority 0.

sections.title: Reading the Answer and Choosing a Protocol
sections.content:
The returned DNS records, if any, specify the next-hop server, which may be a protocol gateway or an endpoint. Systems that register for this DNS-based SRV resolution service list the transfer protocols by which they can be reached, either directly or through a translating gateway, using combinations of Service and Protocol labels as described above. The choice of which IM transfer protocol to use, and therefore to resolve, is a local configuration option for each sending system.

Using this mechanism, seamless routing of IM traffic is possible, regardless of whether a gateway is necessary for interoperation. To achieve this transparency, a separate record for a gateway must be present for each transfer protocol and domain pair that it serves.

The URIs also work in architectures with no gatewaying at all. If a principal's endpoint supports several instant messaging applications, a domain that identifies that host can publish the records described here, so a client that supports only one protocol can look up the record for its protocol and learn how to contact the endpoint. The principal would use an IM URI as its canonical address. Where a service provider runs CPIM or CPP gateways in its own domain that map standard Internet protocols to an internal proprietary protocol, such a gateway can be identified by an IM URI, and the DNS records used to dereference that URI serve a purpose similar to that of Mail Exchange (MX) records.
sections.plainLanguage: The answer names the server to send to next, which may be the endpoint itself or a gateway that translates between protocols. Each sending system decides locally which protocol to use, and the receiving system publishes a record for every protocol and domain pair it serves, so the client can find it either directly or through a gateway.

sections.title: Handling More Than One Address
sections.content:
When the lookup succeeds, the mapping can result in a list of alternative delivery addresses rather than a single address, because of multiple SRV records. For reliable operation, the client MUST be able to try each of the relevant addresses in this list in order, until a delivery attempt succeeds. There MAY also be a configurable limit on the number of alternate addresses that can be tried. In any case, the client SHOULD try at least two addresses.

Resolvers must follow the standard procedures in RFC 2782 for handling the priority and weight fields of SRV records.
sections.plainLanguage: Several servers may be returned, and the client sends to them one after another until one accepts the message. The client may put a limit on how many it tries, but it should try at least two. The order and the weighting between them follow the rules of RFC 2782.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The use of IM and PRES URIs, and the DNS procedures in this document, introduce no security considerations beyond those described in the requirements for instant messaging and presence (RFC 2779) and in the SRV specification (RFC 2782).

Subsequent registrations of Protocol labels for use with the _im or _pres Service labels MUST, however, explain any security considerations that arise from the use of the protocol in question with SRV.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new is introduced here, and the risks stay those of the messaging requirements and of the DNS service record rules. Anyone adding a new protocol label later has to describe the risks of that protocol in the registration.

sections.title: The Two Label Registries
sections.content:
This document reserves the use of the _im and _pres Service labels. Since these relate to a service that may pass messages over a number of different message transports, they must be associated with a specific instant messaging or presence service.

To keep the association between _im and _pres and their underlying services deterministic, IANA created two independent registries: the Instant Messaging SRV Protocol Label registry and the Presence SRV Protocol Label registry. An entry in each registry consists of a label name and a pointer to a specification describing how the protocol named in the label uses SRV. Specifications should conform to the requirements listed in RFC 2434 for 'specification required'.

Protocol labels compliant with this specification MUST begin with the underscore character and follow all other rules for SRV Protocol labels described in RFC 2782.
sections.plainLanguage: Two lists are kept by IANA, one for messaging protocols and one for presence protocols. Each entry is a label starting with an underscore plus a pointer to a document explaining how that protocol uses the DNS service records.
